name: Natufian culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: Hunter-gatherers of the Levant who were among the first people anywhere to live in villages all year round, before farming began. They built round stone-based huts, harvested wild cereals with sickles, buried their dead in their settlements and kept dogs. The oldest known bread-like food, about 14,400 years old, comes from the Natufian site of Shubayqa 1 in Jordan, and people at Abu Hureyra may have begun cultivating rye.

name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic A (PPNA)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: The first stage of the Neolithic in the Levant and Upper Mesopotamia, before pottery was invented. People lived in small round houses of mudbrick and stone, began cultivating crops while still hunting wild animals, and buried their dead beneath their floors. Kathleen Kenyon defined it at Jericho, with its wall and tower; the great pillar enclosures of Göbekli Tepe were built in this time.

name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic B (PPNB)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: The second stage of the aceramic Neolithic, when farming villages spread across the Fertile Crescent and to Cyprus. Houses became rectangular, often with polished lime-plaster floors. Goats, sheep, pigs and cattle were domesticated in northern Mesopotamia during this time. Large villages such as ʿAin Ghazal, Çayönü and Abu Hureyra grew to thousands of people before many were abandoned around 6500 BCE.

name: Capsian culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from stone tools, food remains and radiocarbon dates at sites in Tunisia and Algeria.
summary: Hunter-gatherers of inland Tunisia and eastern Algeria, named after the town of Gafsa (Latin Capsa). At the time the Maghreb was an open savanna. Capsian people hunted aurochs, hartebeest and hares and ate many land snails. They made tiny stone tools (microliths), turned ostrich eggshells into beads and containers, and wore seashell necklaces. They are among the best-known foragers of early North Africa.

name: Yarmukian culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A Pottery Neolithic culture of the southern Levant, among the first in the region to make pottery. It is named after the Yarmuk River near its type site of Shaʿar HaGolan, at the foot of the Golan Heights, where excavators found many clay and stone figurines. It existed alongside other early pottery cultures further south.

name: Hassuna culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: An early farming culture of northern Mesopotamia, named after Tell Hassuna south of Mosul in Iraq. Its villagers grew cereals, kept animals and made painted and incised pottery. Hassuna, Samarra and Halaf pottery styles overlap in time and place, and archaeologists use them to trace how farming communities spread over the plains of northern Iraq and Syria.

name: Samarra culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A farming culture of central Mesopotamia along the middle Tigris, known for finely made pottery painted with stylised animals, including birds, and geometric patterns. At Tell es-Sawwan near Samarra, evidence of irrigation and flax growing shows a prosperous, organised society. Its people were among the first to farm the dry lowlands by bringing river water to their fields, a step toward the later cities of the south.

name: Halaf culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A Neolithic culture centred on the Khabur valley and the plains of southeastern Turkey, northern Syria and northern Iraq. It is famous for some of the finest painted pottery of prehistory, with geometric and animal designs. Halaf-style material is found right across Greater Mesopotamia. The culture is named after Tell Halaf in Syria, excavated by Max von Oppenheim from 1911.

name: Shulaveri–Shomu culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: The first farming culture of the South Caucasus, in what is now Georgia, Azerbaijan and Armenia. Its villages of mudbrick houses have yielded many kinds of wheat and barley, lentils and peas, and cultivated grape, with traces in pottery of some of the earliest known winemaking. Tools were made of local obsidian, bone and antler.

name: Ubaid culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: The first farming culture of the southern Mesopotamian plain, named after Tell al-ʿUbaid near Ur. Ubaid people lived in large unwalled villages of multi-roomed mudbrick houses, irrigated their fields and built the first temples of Mesopotamia, as at Eridu. Over time their painted pottery spread north across Mesopotamia, from the Amuq valley in the northwest to the coast of the Persian Gulf, laying the ground for the first cities.

name: Ghassulian culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A Copper Age culture of the southern Levant, named after Teleilat el-Ghassul near the north end of the Dead Sea in Jordan. Its people lived in small farming hamlets, decorated houses with colourful wall paintings such as the 'Ghassulian Star', buried the bones of their dead in clay ossuaries shaped like houses, and were skilled metalworkers: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of cast copper sceptres and crowns belongs to this time.

name: Badarian culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: The earliest known farming culture of Upper Egypt, named after El-Badari in Middle Egypt. Badarians grew crops, kept cattle, sheep and goats, and gave some animals and dogs ceremonial burials. They buried their own dead in cemeteries at the desert edge with black-topped pottery, ivory figures, shells and amulets. They were the forerunners of the Naqada culture.

name: Naqada culture
evidenceNote: Mostly known from cemeteries and towns dated by radiocarbon; the first Egyptian writing appears only in its last phase.
summary: The Predynastic culture of Egypt, named after the town of Naqada near the gold routes of the eastern desert. Over three phases (Naqada I–III) villages in Upper Egypt grew into towns such as Hierakonpolis and Abydos, crafts and trade flourished, and the culture spread north into the Delta. In its final phase local kings unified Egypt and the first hieroglyphs appeared. A 2013 radiocarbon study suggests it began c. 3800–3700 BCE.

name: Maadi–Buto culture (Lower Egyptian culture)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: The main prehistoric culture of the Nile Delta and the Cairo area, at the same time as Naqada I and II in the south. Named after the sites of Maadi and Buto, its villagers farmed wheat and barley and kept cattle, sheep and pigs. They used copper and imported many goods from Palestine. It was later absorbed as Naqada culture spread north.

name: Uruk culture
evidenceNote: Known from excavated cities; the first proto-cuneiform tablets appear only near its end, around 3400–3300 BCE.
summary: The culture of southern Mesopotamia when the first cities grew up, named after Uruk. Temples became huge, cylinder seals and clay tokens were used to manage goods and workers, and around 3400–3300 BCE the first writing, proto-cuneiform, appeared for record-keeping. In the 'Uruk expansion' its people set up colonies and trading posts up the Euphrates and into northern Syria and Turkey. The map shows the city-states themselves from 3400 BCE.

name: A-Group culture
evidenceNote: The A-Group left no writing; it is known from cemeteries and from Egyptian rock carvings and objects found in Nubia.
summary: The first powerful society of Nubia, between the First and Second Cataracts of the Nile in southern Egypt and northern Sudan. A-Group people farmed, herded and traded with Predynastic Egypt, bartering incense, ebony, ivory, carnelian and gold for Egyptian craft products and goods from the Mediterranean. Rich graves at Qustul and Sayala show they had rulers. The culture peaked around 3100 BCE and declined about 200 years later, perhaps after Egyptian campaigns.

name: Maykop culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A Bronze Age culture of the North Caucasus, stretching from the Taman Peninsula toward Dagestan. Its leaders were buried under large earth mounds (kurgans) with gold, silver and bronze, as at the Maykop kurgan itself. It was contemporary with late Uruk Mesopotamia, and its metalworking, including arsenical copper, influenced the steppe peoples to the north. Ancient DNA suggests they descended from farmers who came from the south, from the South Caucasus.

name: Kura–Araxes culture
dateLabel: c. 3500–2000 BCE (ended earlier in some areas)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates. Some scholars date its start as early as c. 4000 BCE.
summary: Also called the Early Transcaucasian culture, it began on the Ararat plain of Armenia and spread over a huge area of the South Caucasus, eastern Turkey and northwestern Iran, about 1,000 by 500 km, with later offshoots as far as the Levant. Its villagers built mudbrick houses, at first round and later rectangular, and made distinctive black-polished pottery.

name: Umm an-Nar culture (Magan)
evidenceNote: No local writing survives; Sumerian texts mention Magan, usually identified with this region, as a source of copper.
summary: A Bronze Age culture of what is now the United Arab Emirates and Oman, named after an island next to Abu Dhabi. Its people built circular communal tombs of finely cut stone, often next to towers built around water sources. The region, usually identified with Magan in Sumerian texts, supplied copper and diorite to Mesopotamia and traded with the Indus Valley civilisation.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Archaeological Sites of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn

name: Kerma culture (Kingdom of Kerma)
evidenceNote: The Kerma people left no writing of their own; Egyptian texts call their land Kush.
summary: The first great kingdom of Nubia, centred on the city of Kerma in northern Sudan. Growing from about 2500 BCE, it reached its peak between 1750 and 1500 BCE, when it controlled a long stretch of the Nile in Upper and Lower Nubia and allied with the Hyksos against Egypt. Its rulers were buried under great mounds. Egypt's New Kingdom pharaoh Thutmose I campaigned south and destroyed Kerma.

name: Dilmun
evidenceNote: Dilmun is named in Mesopotamian texts from the 3rd millennium BCE, and excavations in Bahrain match those descriptions.
summary: A trading civilisation of the Persian Gulf, centred on the island of Bahrain with the nearby coast of eastern Arabia. Mesopotamian texts describe Dilmun as a land of fresh springs and a stop on the sea route between Sumer and the Indus Valley. Its people left tens of thousands of burial mounds. It was never a large territorial state.
dataNote: It was never a large territorial state, so the map's state layer does not draw it.

name: Garamantes
evidenceNote: Herodotus and later Greek and Roman writers describe the Garamantes, and excavations in the Fezzan confirm their towns and farms.
summary: A Saharan people of the Fezzan in southern Libya who built the first urban society in a major desert not centred on a river; their largest town, Garama, had around 4,000 people. They farmed the desert using foggaras, underground channels that tapped groundwater, which supported a large population. They traded across the Sahara and dealt, sometimes violently, with the Roman province on the coast. Herodotus called them 'a very great nation'.
